newsitem.title: UK: EMU to proceed but unemployment a threat - economist.
newsitem.headline: EMU to proceed but unemployment a threat - economist.

text.p: European Economic and monetary union (EMU) will go ahead with at least eight countries making up a first wave, but its long-term success could be jeopardised by endemically high unemployment, a leading economist said on Thursday.

David Currie, professor of economics at the London Business School and now a Labour peer in the House of Lords, said EMU should survive initial technical hitches and the European Central Bank would quickly develop a sound monetary reputation.

"The euro will be a firm, if not a hard, currency and the EMU zone will enjoy low inflation," he said in a report issued in conjunction with a speech from Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown on Thursday.

But he said the loss of exchange rate flexibility and the constraints placed on fiscal policy by the EU stability and growth pact could cause high European unemployment to linger and possibly intensify in some countries.
If that happened, then the future of EMU would depend on how European Union leaders responded.

"In time...continued high unemployment could weaken the position of the ECB and lead to pressures for change," Currie said. "A failure to respond could generate national pressures and lead to a slow unravelling of EMU and possibly eventually the EU itself."
A successful EMU requires reform of fiscal, welfare and labour market structures to generate greater flexibility in European economies, he said.
That, in turn, would require a freer interpretation of the Stability Pact which lays down fines and punishments for EMU-member countries which do not keep their budget deficits under control.
It would also need changes to labour and welfare policies that discourage employment opportunities.
"With such reforms successfully implemented, the EU could travel towards a sustainable and well-functioning monetary union," he said.
Brown's speech to the Royal Institute of International Affairs echoed many of Currie's themes.
Britain's Chancellor reiterated the government's position that Britain would only sign up to EMU if it was in its economic interest.
But he also said he wanted to put British proposals for economic reform at the heart of the EU agenda.
Those proposals were to open up competition and complete the single market, push a new agenda for employment, to promote more flexible markets and reform the European Commission's finances.
